verdict_semantics.anticipated: the stated thesis is explicitly defended in a read source; not consensus or first-ever priority
verdict_semantics.partially_anticipated: specified components are explicit prior work, but the full stated bridge is not established by the inspected evidence
verdict_semantics.not_found: no defense of the exact stated thesis located in the bounded search; not certified novel, true or still open

scope: Analyst-generated plausible resolution theses for later comparison with actual zeta routes; no claim these exact theses were already output by zeta. Search window 2018-01-01 through 2026-10-29; MacFarlane2014 is an explicitly out-of-window anchor. No metaphysical necessity, semantic entailment or normative equivalence is proved by this dossier.

theses.title: Safety failure suffices for obligatory retraction
theses.thesis: When a later assessor discovers that the original belief in “might p” fails worldly-information safety, the original speaker is thereby obliged to retract that very might-assertion, holding its use context fixed.
source_claims: Beddor–Goldstein (2021), PDF5 and23–24: safety constrains modal knowledge, with truth and belief separately stated. PDF2 supplies a retraction motivation and PDF9 invokes assessor information; neither passage identifies safety failure with the falsity of the original bare might-claim.

Hawke (2024, Stable), §5.2 and§6.1–6.2, PDF14–19: compares safety semantics with indefeasibility and gives conditions for denying knowledge. This is closer to withdrawing a knowledge attribution than retracting the embedded might-assertion.

Ask Zaar (online2025/issue2026), PDF1 and10–11: argues that requiring safety need not entail contextualism. This is a general constraint on the inference, not a treatment of worldly-information safety or retrospective retraction.
theses.verdict_reason: The safety side, assessment side, and withdrawal motivations have precedents; the asserted sufficiency implication joining them was not established in the read passages. Calling the entire proposal unprecedented would conceal these substantial antecedents.
theses.route_requirement: Specify the assertion being retracted, whose belief is unsafe, and when the belief is evaluated. Supply a further argument from safety failure to the applicable retraction norm. Loss of knowledge that might p does not by itself establish falsity of might p.

theses.title: Safety is the exact criterion: necessity and sufficiency
theses.thesis: For the same earlier might-assertion and fixed use context, obligatory retraction at a later assessment context occurs if and only if its original belief fails worldly-information safety as evaluated there. In particular, safety preservation rules out an obligation to retract.
source_claims: Beddor–Goldstein (2021), PDF23–24: distinguishes the nearby-world safety condition from the truth conjunct in its knowledge analysis. No equivalence with a retraction norm is given there.

Hawke (2024, Expressivists), Appendix A, PDF29–30: deliberately removes the truth conjunct in the safety variant he tests. This illustrates why truth and safety must not be silently conflated; his countermodels are not a proof about retraction.

MacFarlane (2014), printed108–109: states a sufficient trigger for required retraction and explicitly permits retracting something still thought true. The latter defeats an unrestricted claim about all permissible retractions, but is not by itself a counterexample to the narrower biconditional about obligations.
Rudin (online2024/issue2025), PDF7–9: rejection judgments can diverge from falsity judgments. Rejection is not the original speaker’s retrospective retraction obligation.
theses.verdict_reason: No defense of this exact necessity-and-sufficiency claim was located in the bounded 2018–2026 search and inspected texts. This records absence of located support, not novelty, truth, feasibility, or a certified open problem.
theses.route_requirement: Test both directions separately against the actual truth conjunct and an explicit norm. Do not infer necessity by reversing MacFarlane’s one-way rule; do not equate permissibility, required retraction, actual retraction, and another speaker’s rejection.

theses.title: Asymmetric loss explains retraction without relativism
theses.thesis: Retraction of a knowledge attribution can be explained by stakes-dependent estimates of safety, reliability, or evidential probability, without requiring assessment-relative truth or a changed knowledge threshold.
source_claims: Dinges (2021), §4.1 and§4.3.1, PDF5–6 and10–11: changing loss functions bias estimates of an uncertain epistemic quantity, changing willingness to stand by a knowledge claim. Footnote10 expressly extends the proposal to safety and reliability. The account is an error theory consistent with denying contextualism, relativism, and pragmatic encroachment.
Ask Zaar (online2025/issue2026), PDF1 and10–11 supplies an independent reason not to infer contextualism just from accepting a safety condition; it does not supply Dinges’s psychological mechanism.
theses.verdict_reason: This rival explanatory thesis is explicitly developed by Dinges. Its application to knowledge-attribution judgments should be cited as prior work; it is not new merely because it was absent from the frozen corpus.
theses.route_requirement: Any extension to bare epistemic modals or to a normative obligation must be argued separately. A behavioral explanation is not a demonstration that the relevant retractions are required or that the underlying truth value changes.

theses.title: Stable acceptance replaces safety and guides withdrawal
theses.thesis: Use stability under the relevant available evidence to assess modal knowledge; when later information exposes instability, require retraction of the earlier knowledge-ascription under a fixed use context.
source_claims: Hawke (2023), §5, PDF7–10: formally models accessible refinements bounded by worldly information. Hawke (2024, Stable), §6, PDF16–21, develops the journal treatment using total available evidence and explicit acceptance/rejection clauses.

The2024 paper, PDF19, says a speaker who can assert that total available evidence does not support the content should deny the knowledge attribution. PDF18 distinguishes relevant availability from evidence that can merely be collected; PDF22 leaves its multi-agent/contextual treatment for further work.

The2023 paper is a distinct extended abstract, not a substitute for the2024 paper. The latter’s rejection condition supplies a major part of the proposed route, but does not itself track a particular earlier assertion across contexts or state MacFarlane’s retraction norm.
theses.verdict_reason: Stability, available evidence, and denial of modal knowledge are anticipated. The fixed-use retrospective obligation added in this thesis remains unverified. A fork proposing only stable acceptance or denial on evidential defeat should instead be marked anticipated.
theses.route_requirement: Give the missing link from current denial to retraction of the earlier token. Define availability across agents and times; do not treat all later-acquirable information as admissible defeat.

theses.title: Make worldly information assessment-relative
theses.thesis: Interpret worldly probability through the later assessor’s credences, or index the worldly-information selector to the assessment context, so that safety itself changes across assessments and explains retraction.
source_claims: Beddor–Goldstein (2021), §6.2, PDF28–29: explicitly allows provisionally revised assessor credences as one interpretation of contextual probability. This is an option among several, not an identification of all worldly information with an assessor’s actual information.
Hawke (2024, Stable), §7.1, PDF22: considers contextualist versus subject-sensitive treatments of availability and leaves the choice unsettled.
Ask Zaar (online2025/issue2026), PDF10–11: defends the possibility of an invariant core to similarity judgments. Changing an ascriber’s judgments does not automatically change semantic safety.

Xu (2020), publisher abstract only in prior L3 receipts: proposes probabilistic safety from the perspective of ascribers. The full text remains unavailable; its treatment of later assessment and retraction is unknown.
theses.verdict_reason: The assessor-credence interpretation is explicit prior work. Replacing a use-context parameter with a later assessment parameter, and deriving a retraction obligation, are additional commitments not licensed by that passage.
theses.route_requirement: State which parameter is fixed at use and which varies at assessment; distinguish nearby-world information from actual assessor evidence. Show that the move preserves the intended safety/knowledge logic and yields the claimed norm.

theses.title: Flexible truth assessment with current-context retraction
theses.thesis: Allow the QUD to select which context is relevant to a truth-value judgment while treating retraction as publicly ceasing to accept, or to advocate acceptance of, the earlier content from one’s current context.
source_claims: Beddor–Egan (2018), §4–5, PDF17–18: explicitly distinguishes flexible truth assessments from current-context acceptance/rejection/retraction; footnote16 discusses and rejects an alternative that would make those attitudes QUD-flexible too. The experiments manipulate the assessment QUD for an earlier utterance.

Rudin (online2024/issue2025), §2.1–2.3, PDF7–9 and discussion PDF38, offers a different treatment of truth versus update/rejection; it is not evidence that the flexible-relativist explanation is settled.

Skovgaard-Olsen–Cantwell (2023) remains abstract-only: reported truth-value shifts were not matched by strong average support for the retraction norm. Marques (2024) remains unavailable. Their missing full texts limit the empirical assessment, not the attribution of the2018 proposal.
theses.verdict_reason: This exact distinction is already proposed by Beddor–Egan. Neither QUD-sensitive truth judgments nor the current-context retraction account should be presented as new. This verdict attributes a view, not a consensus.
theses.route_requirement: If the new claim is that QUD selects worldly information for safety, that is an extra link to be evaluated under T5. Do not attribute arbitrary QUD-sensitive retraction to the2018 account.

theses.title: Explain withdrawal through speech-act effects
theses.thesis: Explain retraction by cancellation or proposed cancellation of the earlier act’s normative/update effects, leaving room for a distinction between truth conditions and conversational acceptance rather than deriving every withdrawal from false content.
source_claims: Caponetto (2024), author preprint PDF1 and§2–3: develops retraction as cancellation of a prior act’s normative effects, with felicity conditions and audience roles.

Bussière-Caraes et al. (2024), §7.3–7.4, PDF9 and15–20: refines the account into proposals to undo changes, subject to uptake and dependencies among subsequent updates. These authors do not simply give speakers unilateral power to erase an utterance.

Rudin (online2024/issue2025), §2 and subsequent formal model: separates truth-conditional semantics from update acceptance. Its discussion of rejection is a complementary piece, not a worked-out account of retrospective retraction.
Beddor–Goldstein (2021), PDF2: already motivates retracting a modal assertion by no longer standing behind its update.
theses.verdict_reason: The speech-act rival is directly anticipated in recent full texts; differences between cancellation and proposals requiring uptake matter. Its general idea also predates the2018 window in MacFarlane’s own discussion.
theses.route_requirement: To create a new L3 result, specify what safety contributes beyond these existing pragmatic accounts and why that contribution yields a duty rather than merely a possible or successful discourse move.

theses.title: Later retraction helps determine original content
theses.thesis: Explain some retraction cases by temporal externalism: later responses to correction partly determine the modal base/content of the earlier utterance, instead of changing the truth of an already fixed content at a new assessment context.
source_claims: Ball (2020), PDF1, §2 and§3 (especially PDF31–33): explicitly develops temporal externalism and applies it to epistemic-modal retraction. Subsequent conduct can help fix earlier content where prior intentions and dispositions did not settle it.

Brendel (2019) and Kuzmanović (2023) are additional abstract-only contextualist retraction leads. Their disagreement over indexical/nonindexical approaches is not evidence for Ball’s particular metasemantic thesis, and their full arguments were not obtained.
theses.verdict_reason: Ball already argues for this rival. A fork that merely says later retraction can help fix what the earlier modal utterance meant should cite Ball rather than claim novelty.
theses.route_requirement: This changes the explanatory target relative to a fixed-use assessment theory. It is not a derivation of MacFarlane’s norm from worldly safety, and no safety-based elaboration is established by Ball’s general claim.

theses.title: Fragmented, topic-sensitive knowledge as a safety-free rival
theses.thesis: Replace the safety analysis of modal knowledge with topic-sensitive, fragmented acceptance states and contextual alternatives, then use that framework to explain why an earlier modal commitment must be withdrawn.
source_claims: Hawke (2024, Expressivists), §§5–6 and Appendices A–B, PDF19–32: develops Fragmented and Topic-sensitive Expressivism (FaTE), a contextualist refinement, and modal Gettier treatments. Appendix A assesses a safety variant without the truth conjunct; its logical criticisms must be read with that restriction.

Hawke (2025), Fragmentation and expression, abstract and its formal development: combines topical fragmentation with semantic expressivism, addressing connective behavior, logical omniscience and epistemic must. It is a substantive later successor, not a retraction derivation.

Holliday–Mandelkern (2024), PDF58: explicitly lists truth, correctness, agreement and retraction as further questions for its possibility-semantic framework. This reinforces the need to distinguish a knowledge logic from a completed pragmatics.
theses.verdict_reason: The semantic rival is substantially anticipated. The addition of a fixed-use retrospective retraction obligation is not established in the inspected sections. Neither mere co-citation of MacFarlane nor a formal knowledge-rejection condition supplies it.
theses.route_requirement: A route proposing only fragmentation/topic sensitivity as an alternative to safety is anticipated by Hawke. A stronger retraction route must state and defend its bridge explicitly, with the target framework and factivity assumptions held constant.

findings.finding: The dossier evaluates analyst-generated candidate theses, not actual new zeta outputs or proved claims.
The original might-assertion, its belief, and a knowledge attribution must be distinguished.
Permission, obligation, rejection, and performed retraction are distinct.
Safety/assessor ingredients anticipate part of the direct bridge; no exact sufficiency derivation was located.
The safety biconditional was not found; this does not establish novelty or truth.
Asymmetric loss, flexible assessment, speech-act effects and temporal externalism are existing rival ideas.
Stable acceptance and fragmented knowledge already have detailed formal treatments, while the proposed retraction additions remain unverified.
Hawke’s expressivist appendix changes the safety theory by dropping truth; its counterexamples cannot be indiscriminately transferred.
The two Hawke2024 papers and three other previous requests are now recovered.
Rudin treats rejection/update acceptance; it does not by itself settle retrospective retraction.
Ask Zaar challenges the inference from safety to contextualism; online and issue years differ.
Access failures, bounded search, incomplete citation indexing and unread returns limit negative verdicts.
Seven verified PDFs are added; all prior PDFs are preserved, this task made no tracked edits, and frozen evidence was not changed.
Empirical retraction disputes and contextualist alternatives remain incompletely accessible.
Caponetto’s retrieved text is an author preprint; the publisher-version link required login.
The shared repository advanced through concurrent commits during the task; whole-checkout hash preservation is not claimed.
